petulance

PET-yoo-lunss · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Petulance is childish irritability or bad temper, especially over small things.

The star's petulance over a minor scheduling change delayed the entire film shoot.

Example

The petulance in his voice was obvious the moment he was told he couldn't have a third helping of dessert.

Being upset about a small, minor thing like dessert -- and sounding sulky rather than genuinely hurt -- is exactly petulance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sulkiness: Sulkiness is a mood of silent, resentful irritation -- the folded arms and pointed quiet after a disappointment. Petulance is noisier and more childish: whining, snapping, and complaining out loud, usually over something small.

peevishness: Peevishness is a standing tendency to be easily irritated over small things -- a peevish person is annoyed by nearly everything, nearly all the time. Petulance is the childish display itself: the whining, sulky temper that erupts over one particular little grievance.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

graciousness: kind and pleasant good manners

Where it sits · how far the bad mood boils over — grumpiness → petulance → tantrum

grumpiness vs. petulance: Ordinary grumpiness is a mild, everyday bad mood; petulance is a more childish, sulky crankiness, usually over something small.

tantrum vs. petulance: Petulance can simmer quietly as sulking; a tantrum is a loud, uncontrolled outburst.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pet

root — pet: to seek or attack (Latin (petere))

suffix — -ulance

suffix — -ulance: full of (Latin (-ulentus))

Put it together

Put it together: Petulance traces back to Latin petere, 'to seek or attack,' plus -ulent -- so petulance was originally a small, snapping 'attack' of crankiness.

Use the root in a new word: appetite

Use the root in a new word: appetite: The same petere root gives us appetite (a 'seeking after' food) and compete (to 'seek together' the same goal).
